lesson.menu_title: If I Had More Time — The Tense for Things That Are Not Real
lesson.menu_desc: A past tense that is not about the past, and the conversation after dinner -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- If I Had More Time
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Janderson Roberto Teixeira | Lesson 13 -- If I Had More Time
lesson.grammar_point: second conditional for unreal and hypothetical situations

listenings.text: If you only ever ask one question at a dinner table, make it this one. If somebody gave you a free year, what would you do with it? People answer that honestly, and they answer it fast, and the reason is simple. Nothing is at stake. Nobody is being asked to commit to anything, nobody is being judged, and there is no wrong answer, so the guard comes down in about four seconds. It also works with a complete stranger, because it asks about a person without asking anything private. And here is the part I find interesting. When somebody gives you the same answer they gave three years ago, word for word, it usually means the thing is not imaginary at all. It is just waiting.

I was in two minds about it for about ten years, which is an embarrassing sentence to say out loud. Every year I told myself the same thing: if I had more time, I would do it properly. My wife finally said the obvious. If you wait for a free year you will wait for ever, and one Saturday a month is already enough. So I started, badly, on somebody else's boat, and I was terrible at it for two seasons. People ask me what I do out there now and the honest answer is mostly nothing. I sit on it and I wind down for three hours. That is not a side effect. That is the entire point.

extra_audio.text: Beth asks Janderson what he would do with a free year. He answers that he would take up sailing and learn it properly. Beth says that is not the answer she expected from him. He explains that he is tied up until seven every day, so it stays imaginary. Beth says that if he started now, one Saturday a month, he would be sailing by the summer.
